To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) perioperative prophylactic antibiotic administration is more cost effective than postoperative antibiotic therapy in the prevention of infection of the wound or peritoneum, (2) the most cost effective prophylaxis is the one that is most likely to achieve the highest possible tissue concentrations at the time of contamination, and (3) the least cost effective prophylactic antibiotic is the one that fails to reach sufficient concentration in the tissue or fluid at risk by that critical time.
(1) prophylactic antibiotic must be administered preoperatively, and (2) postoperative antibiotic is not necessary to further reduce the infection rate in either elective or emergency surgery.

(1) prophylactic antibiotic therapy should be given only when there is a significant risk of infection, (2) it should be administered in a dosage and schedule that will provide adequate tissue levels by the time of anticipated bacterial contamination, and (3) it need not be given beyond the first 24 hours postoperatively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the timing, duration and economics of prophylactic antibiotic therapy.
the timing and duration of antibiotic therapy in surgery and with the economics of infection.
the timing and duration of antibiotic prophylaxis, and its economic implications, in the prevention of postoperative infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of prophylactic antibiotics should be limited to the time of surgery; postoperative antibiotic administration, in the absence of a documented infection, should be avoided because of the increased risk of developing resistant bacterial flora and because of the added expense of unnecessary antibiotic therapy.

perioperative prophylactic antibiotics are indicated for most major surgical procedures, but postoperative administration of these agents should be reserved only for those cases of contaminated or potentially contaminated surgery in which the risk of infection is high and/or the consequences of infection are severe.
prophylactic antibiotic therapy should be administered preoperatively, but that it need not be continued postoperatively in order to be maximally efficacious and cost effective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
perioperative administration of an effective antibiotic is sufficient prophylaxis for most elective and many emergency operations, and postoperative antibiotic is indicated only in selected cases.
prophylactic antibiotic therapy should be given only for the duration of the operative procedure, and that postoperative antibiotic should not be used routinely.
the administration of antibiotics for surgical prophylaxis must be continued postoperatively only in the presence of a specific indication, and then only for the shortest possible time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the administration of antibiotics to patients undergoing elective surgery is an effective and economical way to prevent postoperative wound infection.
the use of antibiotics in surgery is not a simple matter of “more is always better.”
antibiotic prophylaxis should be initiated as early as possible before the operation.
